theory.title: Purpose, scope, and evidence
theory.overview: Digital forensics is a disciplined way to collect, preserve, examine, and explain digital evidence for a defined question. The scope is set by the case, authorization, available data, and the limits of the examination; it is not a license to inspect everything.
teachingPoints: Evidence may be a file, record, device state, log, or other digital observation tied to a question.
Integrity concerns whether the examined bytes or records remained unchanged under the stated controls.
Relevance and reliability are separate judgments: a preserved artifact can still be incomplete, misleading, or unrelated.
A forensic note should name the source, method, time context, and uncertainty.
guardrails: A hash match does not prove authorship, legality, or interpretation.
Local source material is factual reference only; all product expression is original.

theory.title: Lifecycle and forensic readiness
theory.overview: A repeatable investigation moves through preparation, identification, collection, preservation, examination, analysis, and reporting. Readiness happens before an incident through logging, time coordination, retention, asset knowledge, and procedures that make later interpretation possible.
teachingPoints: Preparation defines roles, authorization, scope, contacts, and likely evidence sources.
Identification asks which data can answer the question and what may disappear or change.
Examination extracts observations; analysis relates those observations to the investigative question.
Reporting makes methods, evidence, reasoning, limitations, and conclusions reviewable.
guardrails: The lifecycle is a reasoning model, not a universal legal checklist.
Organizational and jurisdictional requirements must be checked separately.

theory.title: Integrity, repeatability, and boundaries
theory.overview: A useful forensic record separates what was observed from what was inferred and what was concluded. Another qualified examiner should be able to follow the material steps and understand which assumptions, missing data, and controls shaped the result.
teachingPoints: An observation is a recorded property or event; an inference connects observations; a conclusion answers the bounded question.
Repeatability improves when inputs, tools, versions, transformations, and decisions are recorded.
Integrity controls protect the evidence record but cannot repair incomplete collection.
Legal advice and admissibility determinations are outside this general foundation.
guardrails: Do not turn a plausible story into a fact without corroboration.
Use qualitative uncertainty; no numeric confidence model is created here.

theory.title: Identification and acquisition choices
theory.overview: Acquisition begins by identifying the sources needed for the question and the constraints that affect collection. A live system, a powered-off device, a remote log source, and a pre-existing image each present different visibility and change risks.
teachingPoints: Define the target, time window, data categories, authorization, and stopping conditions.
Record whether collection is live or dead-box and what state changes the method may cause.
Consider order of volatility when data may disappear, while documenting the authority and limitations for that choice.
Collect only what is proportionate to the question and retention requirements.
guardrails: No acquisition command or real evidence handling is performed in this Foundation.
A collection plan is not proof that collection occurred.

theory.title: Preservation, imaging, and working copies
theory.overview: Preservation keeps the original evidence protected while analysis occurs on a documented working copy. An image is a representation of storage or selected data; its completeness, format, acquisition method, and verification record must be stated rather than assumed.
teachingPoints: Separate original, acquired image, verified copy, and analyst export in the case record.
Record source identity, acquisition context, operator, tool/version, timestamps, and verification results.
Live collection may be necessary but changes system state and should document those changes.
A working copy can support repeatable analysis only when its relationship to the source is clear.
guardrails: Image format names do not establish completeness or authenticity by themselves.
Use synthetic specifications only; no image is mounted or processed.

theory.title: Hashes, write protection, and custody
theory.overview: A hash digest can help compare bytes at two points in a process. Write protection reduces unintended changes during certain acquisition paths. Chain of Custody records who handled what, when, where, and why; it complements, but does not replace, technical integrity controls.
teachingPoints: Compare source and verification hashes using the same stated byte scope and algorithm.
Distinguish hashing for integrity comparison from encryption for confidentiality and authentication for identity or access decisions.
A hardware Write Blocker, software control, or live-acquisition procedure has context-specific limits.
Custody entries should capture transfers, storage, controls, exceptions, and responsible people or roles.
guardrails: Hash equality does not prove provenance, lawful collection, or analytical correctness.
A Write Blocker is not magical proof that every other control worked.

theory.title: Storage, partitions, and allocation
theory.overview: Storage analysis needs a layered mental model: device or image, partition or volume, filesystem, directories, files, and records. Each layer can expose different metadata and can limit what a higher-level tool is able to interpret.
teachingPoints: A partition describes a region of storage; a filesystem organizes records and data within a volume.
Allocated space is associated with current filesystem allocation; unallocated space is not automatically empty or meaningful.
Offsets, sectors, clusters, and logical paths are different coordinate systems.
Document the layer and transformation used before attaching meaning to an artifact.
guardrails: A tool’s friendly path view may hide lower-layer limitations.
The course teaches interpretation, not storage-driver implementation.

theory.title: Metadata, deletion, and slack space
theory.overview: Filesystem metadata can describe names, locations, sizes, attributes, and times, but those values have semantics and failure modes. Deleted data may remain partly recoverable, while slack space is residual space whose contents and meaning depend on allocation history and interpretation context.
teachingPoints: A deleted directory entry or record is evidence of a filesystem state, not automatically proof of a user action.
Recovery depends on overwrite, allocation, fragmentation, filesystem behavior, and the method used.
Slack-space observations require scope, offset, carving or parsing method, and corroboration.
Keep original timestamp values and state the timezone, clock assumptions, and timestamp meaning.
guardrails: Recovered bytes do not automatically establish ownership, execution, or intent.
Do not infer certainty from one timestamp or one residual fragment.

theory.title: NTFS, MFT, and timestamp interpretation
theory.overview: For this Foundation, NTFS and its Master File Table are treated as bounded technical subjects. An MFT record and its attributes can support metadata interpretation, but the record is not a universal log of human intent and documentation must state the filesystem/version context.
teachingPoints: Microsoft describes the MFT as storing information needed to retrieve files from an NTFS partition.
A file can have records and attributes whose interpretation depends on the filesystem context.
Compare related metadata sources rather than treating one time field as definitive.
Record the documented NTFS scope and avoid extrapolating version-specific behavior.
guardrails: The Microsoft developer note reviewed here is explicitly version-bounded.
An MFT record does not by itself prove that a person opened, created, or transmitted a file.

theory.title: Windows event and Registry context
theory.overview: Windows host examinations may combine event logs, Registry data, filesystem metadata, and security-product records. Each source reflects what was configured, retained, and recorded on that host, so the analyst must preserve source context before correlating it.
teachingPoints: Application, Security, System, and custom logs answer different questions and depend on configured collection.
Registry data can describe configuration and state but does not automatically prove who caused a state.
Event records include source and time context that should be retained with the original record.
Missing or overwritten logs are limitations that should appear in the case record.
guardrails: Windows logging infrastructure and artifact behavior vary by OS generation and configuration.
H04 local structure is not supported by the source package; this is independent design.

theory.title: Execution and user-activity artifacts
theory.overview: Prefetch, LNK files, Jump Lists, browser records, and similar artifacts may provide clues about execution or interaction. They are traces produced by particular software and settings, not direct witness statements.
teachingPoints: Treat artifact presence, absence, and timestamps as observations with collection and version context.
A shortcut or recent-item trace can reflect a path or interaction without identifying the actor.
Browser history, cache, and download records can contain sensitive material and require scope control.
Correlate artifact families with logs, identity records, filesystem data, and case timing.
guardrails: Exact artifact schemas are version-sensitive and must be revalidated before authoring updates.
No browser history or local user data is imported into course artifacts.

theory.title: Corroboration and artifact limits
theory.overview: Host artifacts become more useful when independent sources agree on a bounded event, and less reliable when source configuration, clock state, or collection gaps are unknown. The analyst should record competing explanations before naming a finding.
teachingPoints: Use a source matrix to connect each artifact to the question it can and cannot answer.
Record tool and OS versions when parsing behavior or artifact meaning may change.
Ask whether an administrator, automated process, synchronization task, or shared account offers another explanation.
A finding should state evidence, inference, confidence language, and remaining gaps.
guardrails: Artifact presence is not definitive proof of execution or user intent.
No exact-version claim is canonical without a later currentness check.

theory.title: Volatility and acquisition order
theory.overview: Volatile data can change or disappear when a system runs, shuts down, or is collected. A memory plan therefore weighs urgency, authorization, expected disturbance, and the value of preserving more stable sources first or later.
teachingPoints: Record the observed system state and the time a live collection begins.
Acquisition itself can change processes, memory, network state, and logs.
Order-of-volatility reasoning is a decision aid, not a universal command sequence.
Explain why a chosen order fits the case and what information may be lost.
guardrails: No memory acquisition or live-system command is performed.
Volatile evidence is not inherently more trustworthy than stored evidence.

theory.title: Processes, connections, and modules
theory.overview: A memory view can expose process relationships, network connections, and loaded modules that help explain a host state. These observations need identity, time, symbol or parser context, and corroboration before they support a conclusion.
teachingPoints: A process tree can show parent-child relationships, but unusual structure needs context.
A connection observation links a process and endpoint at a point in the captured state.
Loaded-module observations can suggest a line of inquiry without proving maliciousness.
Compare memory observations with host artifacts and network or authentication records.
guardrails: A parser result is evidence input, not ground truth.
No credential extraction, malware execution, or real memory dump is used.

theory.title: Memory triage and limitations
theory.overview: Memory triage narrows questions and identifies evidence worth deeper examination. It should preserve authorization, source identity, acquisition effects, parser version, and uncertainty, especially when secrets or malware indicators may appear.
teachingPoints: Start with the case question and select observations that can address it.
Separate a triage lead from a validated finding.
Document unsupported or unobservable regions and any symbol, profile, or parser limitation.
Handle possible secrets as sensitive evidence and minimize exposure.
guardrails: The Foundation does not teach credential recovery or malware operation.
Memory results are qualitative evidence and require corroboration.

theory.title: Network and log evidence
theory.overview: Network captures and logs provide different views of activity. DNS, HTTP metadata, authentication events, application logs, and security-product records can be related, but each has its own coverage, retention, and interpretation limits.
teachingPoints: Classify a record by producer, collection path, time scope, and level of detail.
A DNS observation may relate a name and time without proving the resulting application action.
HTTP metadata can show communication context without proving intent or payload meaning.
Authentication success or failure needs account, device, time, and policy context.
guardrails: No uncontrolled network target or live packet collection is used.
Absence from one log cannot establish that an event did not occur.

theory.title: Time normalization and clock issues
theory.overview: A timeline preserves original timestamps while adding a documented normalized view. Timezone, daylight-saving rules, clock skew, source precision, and event semantics can all change the apparent order of events.
teachingPoints: Keep the original value, source timezone or offset, and normalized representation.
Record whether a time means occurrence, observation, ingestion, modification, or parser output.
Use known time references and clock quality to state an uncertainty window.
Do not erase conflicts when two sources disagree.
guardrails: UTC conversion is not the same as proving a clock was correct.
A normalized timeline remains an analytical aid, not an absolute truth.

theory.title: Timeline correlation and gaps
theory.overview: Timeline analysis connects events from multiple sources and makes missing or conflicting evidence visible. A strong timeline shows source provenance and confidence for each row instead of presenting a single seamless narrative.
teachingPoints: Build rows with event time, source, observation, related entities, and interpretation status.
Correlate process, endpoint, account, file, and log observations only when the linkage is justified.
Mark gaps caused by retention, disabled logging, collection scope, or uncertain clocks.
Use alternative explanations when the same sequence fits benign activity.
guardrails: A gap is an uncertainty, not evidence that no event happened.
Tool-generated ordering must be checked against source semantics.

theory.title: Hypothesis and evidence planning
theory.overview: Investigation begins with a question that can be tested. A hypothesis states a possible explanation; an evidence plan names what would support, contradict, or refine it and keeps collection within scope.
teachingPoints: Write the initial hypothesis and at least one plausible alternative.
For each expected observation, state the source, method, and interpretation limit.
Separate raw artifact, interpreted fact, inference, hypothesis, finding, and conclusion.
Update the plan when evidence changes the question or exposes a gap.
guardrails: An initial hypothesis is not a conclusion.
Scope and authorization remain controlling constraints.

theory.title: IOC validation and defensive anti-forensics awareness
theory.overview: An indicator is a lead that needs context and independent checking. Analysts can recognize signs of tampering, log clearing, timestamp manipulation, or obfuscation without turning that awareness into an evasion playbook.
teachingPoints: Check an indicator against independent host, identity, network, or timeline sources.
Treat a known hash, name, or endpoint as a clue whose relevance depends on context.
Record signs of missing, altered, or unexpectedly incomplete data as limitations or investigative leads.
Use defensive recognition language and avoid operational instructions for bypassing controls.
guardrails: No evasion procedure, malware deployment, or destructive action is taught.
A scanner or indicator match is not proof of compromise.

theory.title: Alternatives, confidence, and scope
theory.overview: Good forensic reasoning makes competing explanations and limitations explicit. Confidence is expressed qualitatively and should reflect corroboration, source quality, consistency, and unresolved gaps rather than a fabricated numeric score.
teachingPoints: Compare the leading explanation with benign automation, shared access, clock error, and collection artifacts where relevant.
Use supports, is consistent with, suggests, and cannot establish by itself with care.
A high-confidence bounded observation can coexist with a low-confidence account of intent.
State what additional evidence would change the conclusion.
guardrails: No numeric confidence computation is implemented.
Do not call an alternative impossible merely because one artifact is suggestive.

theory.title: Integrated case workflow
theory.overview: An integrated case record links scope, evidence handling, artifact observations, timeline rows, hypotheses, and findings. The linkages should be traceable without pretending that a synthetic exercise is a real investigation.
teachingPoints: Carry source identity and custody context into each analytical output.
Link a finding to the observations that support it and the alternatives considered.
Keep original values and transformations for hashes, timestamps, and exported records.
Use the same synthetic case facts across modules so new evidence extends rather than contradicts earlier work.
guardrails: All case inputs are synthetic specifications.
No local source file is used as case data.

theory.title: Finding validation and limitations
theory.overview: A finding is a bounded statement tied to evidence and analysis. Validation asks whether the finding answers the scope, uses corroboration, accounts for alternatives, and honestly states what remains unknown.
teachingPoints: Use a finding structure with observation, evidence, analysis, alternative explanation, confidence, limitation, and conclusion.
Check that the evidence was collected and transformed within the stated case boundaries.
Distinguish a technical fact from an attribution or intent claim.
Record gaps and recommended next investigative steps without silently filling them.
guardrails: The course does not make jurisdiction-specific admissibility claims.
Qualitative confidence is explanatory, not a computed score.

theory.title: Technical and executive reporting
theory.overview: A technical report helps another qualified examiner follow the work; an executive summary communicates impact, uncertainty, and decisions without unnecessary implementation detail. Both should preserve the evidence boundary and avoid overstated certainty.
teachingPoints: Include scope, methods, evidence references, findings, timeline, limitations, conclusion, and reproducibility notes.
Use a concise executive summary that names the question, material result, confidence language, and major limitation.
Keep tool names and versions in methodology when they materially affect interpretation.
Separate facts, analysis, assumptions, and recommendations.
guardrails: Reporting is not legal advice or official examination certification.
A polished narrative cannot repair weak evidence or missing provenance.

revisionPolicy: Preserve stable asset identity when the semantic topic remains continuous; use a new version or identity for a material semantic change.
